title: Alloy 6 model of the Blygger 0.3 rules

checks.title: 1a. Local closure check prevents self-containment (version-level reading)
checks.detail: No counterexample — scope: for 3 but 1 Origin, 3 Item, 6 Version, 3 Directive, 4 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..7 steps. If the closure walk follows the transclusions[] of the versions actually baked (recursively, as the data-blyg-* tree records them), no thread can contain — through local hops — a quote of itself. [non-vacuity run Vac_LocalNesting (for 3 but 1 Origin, 3 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..6 steps): instance found] Solve time 188.2s.
checks.scope: for 3 but 1 Origin, 3 Item, 6 Version, 3 Directive, 4 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..7 steps

checks.title: 1a′. Local closure check, item-level reading (each local thread's current transclusions[])
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 3 but 1 Origin, 3 Item, 6 Version, 3 Directive, 4 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..7 steps. All on one origin. A v1 is published. B v1 quotes A v1. C v1 quotes B v1, so C's baked HTML holds B v1, which holds A v1. B is republished as v2 without its quote. A is republished as v2 quoting C. The closure check walks C's current transclusions[] (→ B) and B's current transclusions[] (→ nothing): A is not found, so the publish goes through. But the snapshot actually baked is C v1 ⊃ B v1 ⊃ A v1: A v2's own HTML contains a quote of A — the "silly doubling" the check exists to stop. Sound only if the walk follows the transclusions[] of the versions that were baked, not each item's current version. [non-vacuity run Vac_LocalNesting (for 3 but 1 Origin, 3 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..6 steps): instance found] Solve time 81.4s.
checks.scope: for 3 but 1 Origin, 3 Item, 6 Version, 3 Directive, 4 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..7 steps

checks.title: 1b. Self-containment through a remote hop (cross-origin cycle)
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps. Two origins. O2 publishes thread A v1. O1 imports it and publishes B v1 quoting A v1. O2 imports B and republishes A as v2 quoting B v1. A v2 contains B v1, which contains A v1: A quotes itself through a remote hop. The cycle the spec explicitly permits; 1c shows it is finite. [non-vacuity run Vac_CrossOriginCycle (for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps): instance found] Solve time 23.2s.
checks.scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps

checks.title: 1c. Snapshots are well-founded: no version contains itself
checks.detail: No counterexample — scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 3 Item, 5 Version, 3 Directive, 3 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..7 steps. Over versions (not items) the quotation graph is acyclic: a version can only bake versions that were already published when it was. So every baked document is finite, which is what makes 1b harmless — the spec's claim holds. [non-vacuity run Vac_CrossOriginCycle (for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps): instance found] Solve time 39.9s.
checks.scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 3 Item, 5 Version, 3 Directive, 3 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..7 steps

checks.title: 2. Served is promised: only live + pinned are served; pins survive withdrawal
checks.detail: No counterexample — scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 5 Version, 1 Directive, 1 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps. Every served version is the live one or a pin; every pin stays pinned and served forever, through withdrawal and return; no endcap is ever pinned. Honest caveat: with `served` defined as live ∪ pinned this is close to definitional — what it really checks is that no event in the model (withdraw, republish, return) can remove a pin. [non-vacuity run Vac_PinSurvivesWithdrawal (for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 2 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..6 steps): instance found] Solve time 28.6s.
checks.scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 5 Version, 1 Directive, 1 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps

checks.title: 2b. Withdrawal does not reach other origins' baked quotes
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 2 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps. One origin is enough: thread B v1 quotes A v1; A is then republished as v2 and v1 was never pinned. B keeps serving A v1's words, which A's own origin no longer serves anywhere. The same holds after withdrawal and across origins. The spec chose this (snapshot independence): "retention follows the origin's serving surface" (§13.4) binds readers' stores, not other publishers' baked HTML. Solve time 8.6s.
checks.scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 2 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps

checks.title: 3b. Between polls a reader may hold what the origin no longer serves
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 4 Version, 1 Directive, 1 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..6 steps. The origin republishes an item; a reader that has not polled yet still holds v1, which is no longer served. Ordinary lag, not a violation — retention is bounded only at withdrawal. Shown because 6b/8 build on it: a publisher's studio is such a reader, and what it bakes is what it holds. Solve time 5.7s.

checks.title: 5 (a). ForkFaithful under §5.6 alone: a fork bakes what its source pin baked
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 3 but 3 Origin, 3 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 2 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps. Smallest case, one origin and no grammar issue at all: C v1 is published, B v1 quotes C v1, B v1 is pinned, C is republished as v2, then B v1 is forked as A. The fork copies B v1's content_md, the directive re-resolves to the current snapshot, and A v1 bakes C v2 — not the C v1 the pin shows. (This is the own-origin case Venkat reported before #57.) Across origins the same mechanism yields stale versions, unresolvable directives, and — see 5c — partial quotes turned whole. §5.6 does not promise faithfulness (r6: readers MUST NOT infer resemblance), so this is a gap, not a contradiction. [non-vacuity run Vac_ForkWithQuotes (for 3 but 3 Origin, 3 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps): instance found] Solve time 25.0s.
checks.scope: for 3 but 3 Origin, 3 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 2 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps

checks.title: 5c (a). §5.6 alone: a partial quote stays partial in a fork (any client)
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 3 but 3 Origin, 3 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 2 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps. O2 publishes fragment B v1. O3 (partial-aware) imports it, publishes thread A v1 quoting one passage of B (partial), pins A v1. O2 — whose client predates the 2026-10-03 partial grammar — forks A v1. Its parser treats the attached blockquote as ordinary markdown: the fork C v1 bakes B v1 whole and carries the selection as unverified prose. #49 was admitted as a revision (not 0.4) under #43's test, "readers display baked HTML and never resolve" — true of readers, not of a forker that re-parses another origin's content_md. [non-vacuity run Vac_AwareForkOfPartial (for 3 but 3 Origin, 3 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 2 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps): instance found] Solve time 24.6s.
checks.scope: for 3 but 3 Origin, 3 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 2 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps

checks.title: 5d (a). §5.6 alone: …it does stay partial when the forker knows the grammar
checks.detail: No counterexample — scope: for 3 but 3 Origin, 3 Item, 5 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 2 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps. With a partial-aware forker, a partial quote in the source is partial in the fork (or the fork cannot publish because the passage is gone from the forker's snapshot). So 5c's failure is exactly the grammar gap, nothing else. checks.title: 5e (a). §5.6 alone: a fork's text equals its pinned source's text
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 3 but 3 Origin, 3 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 2 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps. The grammar gap in the other direction: B v1 was written on a whole-only client (O1), so its attached blockquote rendered as an ordinary blockquote under a whole quote of C v1. A partial-aware client (O2) forks it: the same content_md now parses as a partial transclusion, and the fork shows only the selected passage instead of the whole of C. Copying content_md changes the text whenever forker and source differ in snapshots or grammar. checks.detail: No counterexample — scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 3 Item, 5 Version, 1 Directive, 2 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps. checks.title: 5g (b). #57: …and with flattening?
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 3 Item, 5 Version, 1 Directive, 2 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps. One origin: C v1 is published, thread A v1 quotes it, A v1 is pinned, C is withdrawn (never pinned). A v1 is then forked as B (by the same origin here; any origin works). Under #57 the fork is A v1's baked HTML flattened, so C's withdrawn, unpinned words are published afresh under a new id as an ordinary blockquote — although the forker knows C is withdrawn, and although the same publisher could not republish a thread of its own quoting C (publish error, §10.2). Under §5.6 alone (5g a) this cannot happen. Defensible — the pin of A already serves those words forever, the ground on which #57 rejected pin-closure — but it is the "freeze this quote at the withdrawn version" §10.2 says is deliberately not offered, now available through fork. Solve time 18.7s.
checks.scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 3 Item, 5 Version, 1 Directive, 2 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps

checks.title: 6b. Is a partial quote re-checkable at the moment it is published?
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 2 Bake, 2 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps. O1 publishes B v1. O2 imports it. O1 republishes B as v2 (v1 never pinned). O2, not having polled since, publishes thread A partially quoting B v1 — the substring check passes against O2's local snapshot, exactly as the spec requires. But O1 no longer serves v1 anywhere: the "any reader MAY re-check" window is empty from the moment the quote exists. Publish-from-local-snapshot (#26) and re-checkability (#49) coincide only when the quoted version is live or pinned at publish. [non-vacuity run Vac_PartialQuote (for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 3 Version, 2 Directive, 2 Bake, 2 Passage, 5 Int, 1..6 steps): instance found] Solve time 11.6s.

checks.title: 6c. Does a partial quote stay re-checkable?
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 3 but 2 Origin, 2 Item, 4 Version, 2 Directive, 2 Bake, 2 Passage, 5 Int, 1..8 steps. A v1 partially quotes B v1 while v1 is live; B is then withdrawn (or republished) without v1 ever being pinned. From then on no reader can re-check the quote. The spec says this in so many words ("while the origin serves that version"), so it is not a contradiction — but a quote's verifiability is in the hands of the quoted author, not the quoter. checks.title: 8b. A stub's stub_of.version never moves backwards across the stub's versions
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 3 but 1 Origin, 2 Item, 5 Version, 2 Directive, 3 Bake, 1 Passage, 5 Int, 1..7 steps. One origin. A v1, then A v2. The author started stub B while A v1 was current (creation value: v1), and publishes B v1 quoting A — agreement sets stub_of to the baked A v2. B is republished as v2 with the quote removed: read literally, r3 says stub_of "keeps the value set when the stub was created", so it falls back to A v1 — below a version the stub itself baked, and a staleness check now reports more staleness than is true. checks.title: 4c. …but if the watermark is deleted with the stored copy on withdrawal
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 6 Doc, 4 Int, 1..10 steps. The origin publishes v1, then withdraws (v2 endcap). The reader fetches the endcap and — following "SHOULD delete its stored copy" / "drop it from the local archive" — forgets the item, watermark included. A stale cache then replays the v1 body (an origin rolling back would do the same). With no watermark the reader has no record and adopts v1 as the item returning: withdrawn content comes back silently. No rewrite by the origin was even needed. The spec never says the watermark outlives the stored copy. Solve time 1.6s.
checks.scope: for 6 Doc, 4 Int, 1..10 steps

checks.title: 4d. Watermark monotone under the forget-on-delete reading
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 6 Doc, 4 Int, 1..10 steps. By construction of the reading: deleting the record on an endcap drops the watermark to zero. See 4c for why it matters. Solve time 1.4s.

checks.title: 4f. Does a lower-version alarm prove the origin rewrote history?
checks.detail: Counterexample found — scope: for 6 Doc, 4 Int, 1..10 steps. No. The origin publishes v1 and withdraws it (v2 endcap); the reader adopts the endcap; a stale edge cache then returns the v1 body. The reader raises the history-rewrite alarm though the origin never rewrote anything. §13.3 does call a lower version the origin's violation (it served an old body), so this is a calibration note, not a bug: surfaced discrepancies will include cache artefacts. Solve time 1.0s.
